title: Electrochemically Induced Intraparticle Separated States in LFP Probed with STEM-EELS
content: Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP)-based batteries are of great importance in energy storage applications due to their high safety, high power density and energy density, as well as their durability. In this study, we use Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS) to evaluate the oxidation state of Fe in a LiFePO4 material that was subjected to a particular high-current stimulus, which considerably increased the number of LFP particles exhibiting intraparticle phase separation. This effect aligns with the thermodynamics-based description of the finite-rate phenomenon of entering the voltage hysteresis loop, hence evidencing that intraparticle phase separation is a consequence of high-current stimuli. A detailed analysis of the Fe²+/Fe³+ mixing level in the LFP and FP phases would be shown, specifically the degree of Fe²+/Fe³+ mixing at the intraparticle LFP/FP phase boundaries obtained from STEM chemical mappings of high-current-activated LFP particles, revealing that the degree of Fe²+/Fe³+ mixing within the particles is very low. Therefore, suggesting that for the high-rate performance of phase-separating insertion materials, the existence of large amounts of nonequilibrium phases is not compulsory. These results indicate that the presence of the solid-solution LixFePO4 phases correspond to a part of the LFP material that has not yet totally relaxed into the corresponding Li-rich and Li-poor phases and that is probably not the reason for the high-rate performance of the LFP material [1, 2].
